children: Stephen is changing—he chooses to take “little part in the games.”
Notice the diction here, as the manner of the games is described as having “romped noisily”, a relatively harsh portrayal of a “children’s party”.

Stephen also sees himself somewhat alienated from “their merriment”, finding “himself a gloomy figure amid the gay cocked hats and sunbonnets.” Stephen determines his sentiment here by comparing his actions to his peers—in this instance specifically, the other children.

Yes, a man ACTUALLY went to a prostitute not for sex, but for emotional support during a vulnerable state.
To prove my argument as I was googling “a man crying in a woman’s arms” the only photos that appeared in the search were these…

If only someone was there to capture this exact moment between Stephen and his lady of the night for google’s sake. Well, at least Joyce shows that it is possible for a man to need or rely on a woman for emotional strength and support!

range.content: Words which he did not understand he said over and over to himself till he had learnt them by heart: and through them he had glimpses of the real world about them.

6320150.twitter_share_message: “Alongside his father and Uncle Charles, Stephen feels his own youth and lack of understanding tr…” —@Genius

annotatable.link_title: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (Chap. 2) by James Joyce
annotatable.title: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (Chap. 2)

children: Alongside his father and Uncle Charles, Stephen feels his own youth and lack of understanding tremendously. He struggles to follow their conversations, learn their vocabulary, and absorb the “real world” they are discussing about, waiting for the moment of his own adulthood, but as far as we can tell, he has no understanding of what that grown-up life involves. This is a recurring theme of the powerlessness of youth, and later this continued powerlessness will ignite a fire in Stephen’s soul. Also, notice that Stephen already has a sense of some “great part” that he’ll play in the world. Someone needs to get off their pedestal…Giving grandeur to himself is perhaps just a part of his nature.

children: ‘Uncle Charles, puffing away at his pipe in the outhouse he calls “his arbour” is a Namer, and deserves  to have something named after him. So, let us designate the Uncle Charles Principle:
the narrative idiom need not be the narrator’s

The Uncle Charles Principle may extend from diction to syntax. Syntax maps a set of judgments about relatedness, and such judgments help define the people who-make them. So Joycean syntax may mirror the priorities of a character we needn’t think of as framing the sentence.’
-Joyce’s Voices, Hugh Kenner, p18.

children: This excerpt comes from Stephen’s attempt to relive the time he spent with E.C. –a woman who he met at the children’s party at Harold’s Cross, with whom he shares his first crush– through a poem.  The initial finishing of the poem shows the development of Stephen as a writer, because before when he tried to write a poem about Parnell, he failed.  However, through the process of writing and the success of finishing it gave Stephen a boost of self-confidence.  Thus developing his character as a teenager who’s slowly but surely finding himself in his own messed up world.
